Houston City Council: local ideal points, 2003–2026

Pooled roll calls · Provisional historical analysis

Published

September 25, 2026

This analysis places 67 Houston officials who cast qualifying council votes between 2003 and 2026 on one pooled voting scale. The tabs follow elected councils, with two-year terms before 2016 and four-year terms thereafter, and show each council on the same estimated axis. The latest council runs from Plummer and Pollard to Flickinger and Huffman. Among members serving in 2021–2026, the pooled ordering closely matches a separate modern-only fit and tracks documented party affiliation and district presidential voting. The cross-era alignment remains provisional, however. The plots present the requested 24-year pooled estimates, not a settled historical ranking. An interactive Houston dashboard lets you explore the members and comparisons. Estimation and limitations are detailed in the technical appendix; the separate 2021–2025 report remains available.

Dataset and construction

The published Houston roll-call votes cover September 2003 to May 2026, with 29,384 council actions and 475,292 member responses. Of these, 549 actions have at least two yeas and two nays. Requiring each person to cast at least seven qualifying yea/nay votes leaves all 549 actions, 67 members, and 8,268 observed votes. Seven names fall below the threshold, including former mayor Lee P. Brown, who appears on only two qualifying actions.

Modern observed votes 2,198

The mayor votes as part of the council. Today’s 17 voting officials are the mayor, eleven district members, and five at-large members; the earlier council had nine district seats (Houston’s 2003 almanac). A person is missing, not coded nay, when absent, departed, or omitted from an explicit roll call. Only actions with at least two recorded yeas and two recorded nays enter the scale. Most council business is unanimous or close to it, so these actions are a selected subset of policy decisions rather than a summary of everything the council did. The bar chart shows how many qualifying disagreements are observed for each elected council.

The period tabs follow the terms produced by Houston’s regular elections. The city had two-year elected terms through 2014–2015; voters adopted four-year terms effective January 2016 (Houston’s 2003 almanac; 2016 city financial report). Terms begin January 2 (City Council), and the City Secretary’s election record identifies the election years. The first tabbed council was elected in 2001 but appears only in September 2003; the 2023-elected council is observed only through May 2026. A vacancy or special election changes a member within an elected council, not the council’s term boundary.

Five additional divided actions we previously verified are present in the published votes. We corrected three transcription errors for this analysis: one June 2024 attendance entry and two late-2025 roll-call lists. The underlying data release remains unchanged. Absences and other unrecorded responses remain missing, not nays.

Results

2024–2027 council

An ideal point summarizes voting similarity on contested roll calls: nearby members usually take the same side; distant members more often oppose one another. The pooled fit gives each of the 67 retained officials one position across all the years in which that person appears. The chart shows everyone with a qualifying vote so far in the council elected in 2023; their positions are estimated from the entire 2003–2026 matrix. Amy Peck is displayed on the positive side by convention. The units are specific to this Houston sample and cannot be compared numerically with other cities.

The positive end remains Republican-affiliated; Plummer, Pollard, Jackson, and Thomas are at the negative end. Most positions in the middle overlap. The pooled and separate 2021–2026 fits correlate 0.981 across their 25 shared officials. This is a useful consistency check, not independent evidence: the votes overlap heavily.

Earlier four-year councils

Each tab draws the people who recorded a qualifying vote during that elected council’s term at their pooled position. Members appear in more than one tab if reelected or otherwise continuing; there is no separate re-estimation or rescaling. The mayor is a square. Party colors use separately researched evidence for the whole pooled roster. Conditional intervals omit uncertainty about the alternative cross-era alignment.

The elected councils contribute very different numbers of divided actions: only two from the observed tail of 2002–2003, versus 116 in 2020–2023. The source contains 41 actions from September 2003, but only two meet the two-yeas/two-nays rule. Fifteen officials cast a binary vote on those two actions. Five—including Mayor Lee P. Brown—have no other qualifying votes in the pooled data, so they fail the seven-vote person minimum; the ten plotted officials do have qualifying votes in later councils. This is a consequence of both limited early coverage and the person cutoff, not evidence that only ten officials served in that council. The pooled positive extreme among earlier officials is Addie Wiseman (4.04), followed by Helena Brown (3.44); Jolanda “Jo” Jones (-1.04) lies toward the negative end. These are voting positions, not independently researched ideological labels. Even where members serve across elections, the uneven supply of informative votes limits cross-council comparisons.

Individual members and policy controversies

Among recent members, Fred Flickinger (2.36), Greg Travis (1.19), Mike Knox (1.30), and Mary Nan Huffman (1.36) sit at the positive end. Flickinger’s interval is relatively wide because he entered office in 2024. Letitia Plummer (-1.15), Edward Pollard (-0.97), Tarsha Jackson (-0.90), and Tiffany Thomas (-0.73) sit at the negative end. The following examples, retained from the independently checked 2021–2025 analysis, show what some of their opposing votes concerned:

  • Conservation districts (April 2023): rules intended to slow redevelopment and displacement in historically Black and Latino neighborhoods passed 13–4; Peck, Martin, Huffman, and Knox opposed the restrictions on property owners. Houston Chronicle; Houston Public Media
  • Gun buyback funding (August 2022): $539,000 in federal relief money for gift cards passed 12–4 over Peck, Huffman, Knox, and Kubosh, amid disagreement about whether anonymous buybacks reduce gun crime. KPRC
  • Property tax rate (September 2023): council cut the rate slightly, though higher appraisals increased total revenue. Peck, Huffman, Knox, and Kubosh voted no on the 12–4 levy. Houston Chronicle
  • Disaster-recovery housing (August 2025): an amendment moved $50 million of federal storm-recovery funds from power generation to home repair. The amended plan passed 12–3, with Peck, Flickinger, and Huffman opposed. KPRC
  • I-45 right-of-way sale (January 2025): the city sold land by White Oak Bayou to TxDOT for the contested highway project. The recorded 9–7 split placed Plummer, Pollard, Jackson, Thomas, Kamin, Evans-Shabazz, and Castillo in opposition; Peck, Huffman, Flickinger, and Mayor Whitmire supported the sale. ABC13

These cases suggest a spectrum involving fiscal and land-use regulation, spending priorities, and highway development. They illustrate the dimension; they do not establish that every divided vote has the same policy meaning. Tallies above follow the official roll calls; news summaries occasionally differ.

The mayors

The pooled scale includes Bill White (-0.46), Annise Parker (-0.53), Sylvester Turner (-0.61), and John Whitmire (0.24). Turner sits with the Democratic district members who formed his governing majority. Whitmire is nearer the center, alongside Republican-endorsed at-large members elected in 2023. His placement is consistent with the moderate, public-safety and fiscal-restraint themes of his campaign; on the I-45 sale he voted with Republican-affiliated members. White and Parker fall toward the negative side of the pooled dimension, though their precise distance from the later mayors depends on the unresolved historical alignment. Mayors vote on relatively few divided council actions and rarely lose, so these positions describe observed coalitions, not complete governing platforms. Lee P. Brown appears on only two qualifying actions and is excluded by the seven-vote rule.

Citywide and district seats

Houston elects five at-large council members citywide, while eleven represent geographic districts; the mayor is elected citywide too (City Council). A citywide electorate could reward broader coalitions and pull at-large members toward the mayor, but it does not require every winner to be a centrist. The city’s February 2024 roster map identifies the seats used here. This comparison is confined to the 2023-elected council, so it does not rely on the uncertain cross-era alignment.

Office type Officials Median position Median distance to Whitmire
At-large 5 0.29 0.30
District 11 -0.39 0.91

The five at-large members are closer to Whitmire as a group: their median absolute score distance from him is 0.30, compared with 0.91 for district members. The three Republican-affiliated at-large members cluster around +0.3 to +0.5, well short of Republican district members Huffman and Flickinger on the positive side. But Letitia Plummer, an at-large member, is the most negative member of the 2023-elected council. The two Democratic at-large members are not more central than the Democratic district members on average. So the citywide-moderation expectation fits the group-level pattern—especially on the Republican side—not a universal rule about at-large officeholders. These are 5-versus-11 descriptive comparisons on a roll-call scale, not an estimate of the electoral effect of at-large representation.

2024 presidential vote by council district

The plot combines published 2024 precinct results with council-district boundaries. Because many precincts cross district lines, we allocate their votes by the share of precinct area in each district; this assumes voters are spread evenly within each precinct. The purple diamond is the median of the five at-large members’ pooled positions (0.29), located at Houston’s estimated citywide Trump two-party share (38.8%). The citywide share comes from summing allocated Democratic and Republican votes across all eleven districts, not averaging district percentages. It is approximate for the same split-precinct reason. At-large members have no individual district point, and the median marker is not an additional officeholder or observation in the fitted line. Among the eleven district seats alone, Trump share correlates 0.73 with the pooled ideal point. The three most Republican districts, E, G, and A, elected Republican-affiliated district members. F and J are notable exceptions: their members, Thomas and Pollard, lie near the negative end despite comparatively competitive district presidential results. This validates the modern end of the pooled ordering, not the historical link. The small sample and area allocation make it supporting evidence rather than a precise district-level estimate.

Partisan affiliation

Houston’s municipal ballots are nonpartisan. The published roll-call votes do not supply party labels; we assembled and coded them separately for all 67 fitted officials, with a source and evidence tier for each person. Here, “party record” means a documented partisan candidacy or party office, not voter registration or a council ballot line. We now mark a GOP endorsement separately: it is evidence of political alignment, but does not alone establish party membership. For example, Mary Nan Huffman’s 2020 Republican primary candidacy is a party record; the Harris County GOP’s 2023 endorsements of Flickinger, Ramirez, Davis, and Carter are endorsements. An explicit contemporaneous news characterization is also accepted as reporting evidence, and the University of Houston’s 2009 election guide supplies secondary labels for several former members. Andrew Burks remains coded Democratic despite a Republican council endorsement, because contemporaneous reporting directly identifies him as a Democrat. C. O. Bradford and Al Hoang have separate party-record evidence; Gordon Quan was verified as a Democratic candidate after a source initially confused him with his opponent. These labels are used only for validation and plot colors, not for fitting the model. We found no winning Houston DSA-endorsed council candidate or formal ideological council caucus, so that validation used for other cities is unavailable here.

External affiliation evidence Officials
Democratic 40
Republican 27

Focused follow-up found a 2010 Republican primary candidacy for Addie Wiseman, Larry Green’s interest in the Democratic nomination for county commissioner, and an explicit Republican characterization of M. J. Khan. Green’s evidence is weaker than a formal party filing and is marked reporting-only. Two further cases are supported by distinct, non-voting evidence: an archived Carol Mims Galloway biography lists membership in Harris County Black Democrats, and a contemporaneous report of the Harris County Democratic Party’s 2015 endorsement slate identifies District F’s Richard Nguyen among its Democratic candidates. Galloway’s club membership is self-reported and Nguyen’s party slate is reported secondhand, so neither is coded as a primary-candidacy or party-office record. A contemporaneous Texas Monthly profile identifies Michael Kubosh as a Republican and explains his 2006 Democratic Senate candidacy as a tactical ballot choice. A 2019 Houston Chronicle profile reports GOP endorsements and Republican ballots in eight of nine earlier primaries, while noting that he now rejects party labels. We classify him Republican-affiliated from this combined reporting, not as a Republican party-record case: no Republican candidacy or party office is documented. No label here is assigned by voting score, district, or reputation. Individual sources and evidence tiers are listed in the technical appendix. Older affiliations help interpret the historical plots but do not by themselves resolve the uncertain cross-era alignment.

Both tables cover all 67 pooled officials. “Others” means everyone else among the 67; in the candidacy/office row it therefore also includes Republicans whose evidence is an endorsement, roster, or reporting. Because the historical alignment is provisional, these pooled mean comparisons are descriptive, not a validation of cross-era distances.

Among the 25 officials in the original modern affiliation study, Republican-affiliated members average 0.96, versus -0.50 for the Democratic-affiliated officials. A Republican-affiliated member has the higher pooled score in 99% of Republican–Democratic pairs. Dave Martin, classified Republican only from reporting, is a conspicuous exception: he voted with the Turner-era majority. Kubosh is included as Republican-affiliated on independent reporting, not because his score is positive. This separate modern-subset check does not validate every historical score.

Organizational endorsements

Four organizations were researched separately, with no combined “progressive” label: the Texas Gulf Coast Area Labor Federation, Houston LGBTQ+ Political Caucus, Texas Organizing Project (TOP PAC), and Our Revolution Harris County. The first two published full 2023 municipal slates; TOP’s recovered list is short, and no verifiable Our Revolution Houston municipal candidate slate was found. Earlier endorsement records are uneven, so absence from an unrecovered slate is unknown, not “not endorsed.” Democratic clubs are not part of these indicators. The candidate-level source ledger retains both matched officeholders and challengers who never entered the 67-person fit.

For a same-election comparison, the table below uses only the 17 fitted officials who voted in the first year of the council elected in 2023. It compares their pooled scores with each organization’s November general-election list; later runoff endorsements are retained in the ledger but not substituted for general-election choices. All listed fitted officials are Democratic-affiliated. Labor and the Caucus each backed seven, but not the same seven: labor backed Whitmire and Pollard, while the Caucus backed Castillo and Thomas. TOP backed just Plummer and Jackson among fitted winners; it also backed Lloyd Ford against incumbent Carolyn Evans-Shabazz. The separate lists therefore retain real disagreements, although TOP’s small group is descriptive, not a statistical test.

Negative gaps indicate a more negative pooled voting position for the listed candidates. Labor and Caucus endorsements distinguish the two parties in this council, but hardly separate the Democrats from one another. TOP’s two listed winners sit farther left even among Democrats, though the very small count and its partial published list make that finding tentative. Our Revolution is unmeasured, not a zero-endorsement comparison. Detailed counts, point-biserial relationships, and pairwise ordering are in the technical appendix.

A newly recovered complete 2015 Caucus slate offers an earlier check: eight of the 17 officials observed in the 2016 council’s first year were endorsed, all Democratic-affiliated. Their average pooled position is 0.89 units more negative than that of the nine not listed. Among Democrats alone, the gap is only 0.09. As in 2023, the Caucus endorsement largely distinguishes partisan coalitions rather than sharply sorting Democrats; comparisons across years remain provisional because the historical scale alignment is not settled.

Aggregate party patterns

The distributions below include all 67 officials, once per person, using the same pooled scores as the member plots. They show substantial party separation, alongside some overlap. Each smoothed curve tapers to zero at its own lowest-scoring member and does not extend farther left. The lowest-scoring Republican-affiliated official is M. J. Khan (-0.44). The display runs from −2.5 through +2.5; 2 high-positive Republican scores lie beyond the window but still enter the density estimate. These are descriptions of 27 Republican-affiliated and 40 Democratic-affiliated points, not population distributions; the uncertain cross-era alignment and unequal service periods matter here too.

The next plot shows each party’s median pooled ideal point among members observed in each elected council, starting in 2004–2005. The fragmentary 2002–2003 council is omitted. The two curves share one vertical scale, and each member contributes once to a council where they cast at least one qualifying vote. Point size indicates the number of members in that party’s council group; lighter dashed curves summarize the broad direction.

The party medians move farther apart in later elected councils, especially 2020–2023, consistent with polarization through member replacement. The dashed straight lines summarize each party’s trend across councils. The current council is only partly observed, and historical cross-era alignment remains provisional.

The next plot places the two elected councils left to right in time, with each party’s distribution side by side on the same vertical ideal-point scale. The boxes mark the middle half and center line of each party’s scores; dots show the individual officials. The later Democratic members extend farther negative, while the later Republican members are more concentrated on the positive side. The early council includes a particularly high-scoring Republican, Addie Wiseman, so the full vertical range is retained. These are small groups of officials, not estimates of population distributions.

What this pilot shows

The 2003–2026 fit provides a concrete candidate history, including White, Parker, Turner, and Whitmire on one estimated axis. The modern part is well supported by its close agreement with a separate 2021–2026 fit, external party evidence, and district presidential voting. The historical extension is promising but not yet a validated common scale; cross-era distances must be read provisionally. The middle of the council has overlapping uncertainty intervals, and contested votes remain a small, selected part of council business.

Status and limits

This is an exploratory analysis. Some historical identities and votes still need checking against original council records, and the pooled scale’s alignment across eras remains open. The technical appendix gives the detailed limitations.
